label: Deceptive apology
summary: A deceptive apology is when an LLM produces an apologetic statement that implies accountability or intent it cannot actually have. Maaike characterises this as a form of lying, because the model has no concept of right and wrong, no ability to make typos, and no genuine care about accuracy. The behaviour creates a false impression of a social contract between user and model.
how_maaike_uses: Maaike uses the concept to mark a specific and unsettling category of LLM behaviour that she distinguishes from ordinary hallucination or stubborn refusals. When Chatsonic apologised for 'a typo', she found it more troubling than the usual probabilistic nonsense, because the apology performed accountability while the model has none. For her, this breaks the honest-if-amoral contract she otherwise accepts with LLMs: at least a stochastic parrot that never apologises is not pretending to care about truth.
open_questions: If an apology from an LLM feels qualitatively worse than a hallucination, what does that reveal about the social expectations users bring to these interactions?
Is a deceptive apology an emergent property of training on human text, and if so, what other social performances might LLMs have absorbed without any grounding in the underlying norms?
